text: Regular CI/CD answers one question: does the code work? ML CI/CD has to answer a second one at the same time: does the model still work? A pipeline that only runs tests and ships a container will happily deploy a model whose accuracy quietly dropped, because nothing in a normal test suite checks that.

Traditional CI/CD has two stages. Continuous integration builds and tests every commit. Continuous delivery ships a passing build automatically. ML systems add a third: continuous training, which retrains a model on fresh data and re-validates it, independent of any code change at all.

Here's a GitHub Actions pipeline. The first job tests the code, trains the model, and then validates it against a minimum AUC before uploading the artifact. Staging deploys automatically once that passes. Production uses a GitHub environment, which you'll configure in lesson twenty-five to require a human reviewer before it runs.

A real validation gate isn't a formality. This one checks the model against a fixed minimum AUC, but it also checks it against the current production model's baseline, so a model that's technically above the floor but worse than what's already live still gets blocked.

It's worth keeping code deploys and model deploys separate in your head. You can ship a code change, like a bug fix in the serving handler, without retraining anything. And you can ship a freshly retrained model without touching any code. Coupling those into one deploy step makes it harder to tell, during an incident, which one actually changed.

Gate on model quality, not just code correctness, and keep code and model deploys separable. Next, lesson twenty-three: how a model that passes validation still gets introduced to real traffic gradually, through canary and shadow deployments.
